blocks.text: Excel for operations managers on Mac covers the same jobs as Windows: capacity plans, shift schedules, reorder lists and weekly reports. The differences sit in the keyboard, a few features that reach Mac later, and the menus. Trouble starts when you guess at a shortcut, or when a tutorial shows a menu that is not where you expect it. This guide covers setup, shortcuts, a worked capacity check and the limits. It ends with where Lazur fits, and what it does not do.
What operations managers keep in Excel on Mac

Most ops teams keep four kinds of workbook. The first tracks capacity: hours of work against hours available, by week and by work center. The second is the shift roster, with names, roles and the gaps in coverage. The third covers inventory, with stock on hand, stock on order and what needs buying. The fourth pulls the other three into a report for the weekly meeting.

Templates can save a morning. User Solutions offers a free capacity planning workbook in .xlsx format with no macros. It has six sheets, a load against capacity view across eight weeks, and a bottleneck ranking. The same page promotes paid software from the same company. Use the free file as a starting point, and rebuild the logic in your own tables before you rely on it.
How much time operations work spends in spreadsheets

A 2022 survey of 1,001 office workers in Australia, the UK and the US found that the average knowledge worker spends more than 20 hours a month in spreadsheets. The same survey found that 40% of workers often struggle to make sense of their spreadsheet data. ThoughtSpot commissioned it, and it covers office workers in general. It does not cover operations managers. Use the figures as a rough signal, not a measure of your week.

Vendor numbers can run much higher. A 2018 article in The Global Treasurer, written by a Kyriba employee, estimated that treasury teams waste an average of 4,812 hours a year on traditional spreadsheets. That figure is for treasury teams, and it comes from a company that sells treasury software. Read it as an example of what a spreadsheet habit can cost, not as a benchmark for your team.
Set up the workbook so it holds up at month end

Start with one table per data set. A table keeps its structure as you add rows. Formulas that point at a table grow with it, so your totals keep up without a manual range edit. Microsoft's October 2026 update says you can name a table as you create it, and that works on Windows and Mac. Pick names a colleague can read without asking, such as shift_roster or stock_on_hand.
Habits that keep the file clean

items: Put one kind of data in each table, with one header row and no blank rows inside it.
Store dates as real dates. Text that looks like a date sorts in the wrong order and breaks weekly sums.
Name each table when you create it, so formulas read as plain English.
Keep inputs on one sheet and calculations on another. Label both sheets in the first cell.
Save a copy before a large paste. Use ⌘Z to undo one step at a time, then check the result.

blocks.text: Mac shortcuts that differ from Windows

Microsoft's Excel for Mac shortcut page uses Option everywhere the Windows list uses Alt. Many Ctrl shortcuts from Windows also work with Control on Mac. Microsoft is clear that not all of them do. Some shortcuts take Command, some take Control, and a few exist only on Mac. Do not assume a shortcut works until you have tried it on a copy of your file.

blocks.title: Build a cheat sheet
blocks.text: Copy the shortcuts you use most into a note, and keep it in a pinned window near your keyboard. Test each one once. A shortcut you cannot remember is no faster than the menu.
Worked example: a weekly capacity check on Mac

Say you track work in a table called Load. Each row is one job, with a work center, a week and the hours it needs. A second table, Capacity, holds the hours each work center can supply that week. The check is simple. Total the load for each work center in each week, then subtract the capacity. A negative result means that week is over capacity.

Build the grid on a summary sheet. Put weeks across the top row and work centers down the first column. In the first cell of the grid, use a formula like =SUMIFS(Load[Hours],Load[Work center],$A2,Load[Week],B$1). Copy it across and down. Build a second grid that subtracts the capacity table from it, and format the negative cells in red.

Two edge cases catch people. First, the week labels must match exactly. A label with a trailing space returns zero, and nothing warns you. Second, the grid shows hours, not cost. A work center with little spare time can still be less risky than one that holds a single late order. Add a column for what a delay costs before you rank anything.
Shift schedules and the formulas that break

For a shift roster, keep one row per person per shift. Put the date, the shift, the role and the site in their own columns. Then use Data > Sort & Filter > Filter to add filter arrows to the header row. Coverage becomes a count with a filter, which is easy to explain to a manager and easy to check.

items: Merged cells break sorting and filtering. Use Center Across Selection or plain columns instead.
A name typed with an extra space becomes a second person in a pivot table.
SUBTOTAL can skip hidden rows, while SUM cannot. Pick the one that matches what you want.
Dates typed as text sort in the wrong order, even when they look right.
A coverage check that reads a blank as covered hides the gaps. Test the formula against a shift you know is empty.

blocks.text: Pivot tables for ops reporting on Mac

A pivot table turns the roster into a coverage count in a few steps. Put the work center on rows, the date on columns and a count of names in the values. The full walk-through is in our [pivot table guide](/how-to/make-a-pivot-table-in-excel). Clean the source table first. A pivot table only groups what you give it.

Pivot tables have limits too. Microsoft's limits page says each PivotTable field can hold up to 1,048,576 unique items. It caps report filters and value fields at 256 each. A report that needs anything near that many filters is a sign to split the data, not to add more filters.
Know the Excel limits before the file gets big

Microsoft's specifications page lists a worksheet maximum of 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns. Most ops files never get near that. In practice, file size and formula count tend to matter first. The same page describes a 32-bit environment with 2 GB of address space. It does not mention Mac, so do not treat those memory notes as Mac facts.

If a monthly file grows past what you can open comfortably, split it by site or by quarter. Keep one summary workbook that links to the rest. Test the split on a copy first, because links break when files move.
Copilot agent mode in Excel on Mac: what is ready

Agent Mode is Microsoft's AI feature inside Excel. Microsoft announced it as generally available on Windows on January 27, 2026, and said Mac would roll out over the coming days. A later line in the same post says it is generally available on Mac too. The two lines conflict, so check your build before you plan around it.

Access depends on your license. Commercial Microsoft 365 Copilot licenses qualify, and so do Microsoft 365 Personal, Family and Premium subscriptions. The Personal and Family plans use an AI credit model. At launch the feature was not offered in the EU or the UK. Microsoft's October 2026 post says its clean data skill is rolling out to general availability on all platforms, while the skill recorder is still Insider only on Mac.
Mistakes operations managers make on Mac

items: Trusting a shortcut from a Windows video without testing it on your Mac.
Writing a reorder formula over a fixed range, so new rows fall outside it. Use a table instead.
Leaving blank header cells in the source data, then building a pivot table on top.
Pasting a supplier or pay column into a chatbot as a screenshot, without checking company rules.
Waiting for a feature that Mac does not have yet, such as the skill recorder, instead of using the menu path that works now.

blocks.text: Where Lazur fits in an Excel session

Lazur is a voice assistant that lives in the notch on your Mac. Hold Option and Command together to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where a button is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do something, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click. Lazur never clicks for you.

The work around the spreadsheet is where a voice helper saves time. Hold fn to dictate a note to the warehouse lead at the cursor, in any app. Ask Lazur to draft a reorder email from the low-stock rows you have open. Ask it to set an Apple Reminders item for Thursday morning. Research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs, through the Lazur for Chrome extension, and comes back as a summary and a report.

Lazur can also explain a formula. Select the cell that shows an error, hold Option and Command, and ask why. Lazur reads what is on screen. It can point at the part of the formula that looks wrong, then talk you through the fix.
Privacy: what Lazur sees and sends

Lazur listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so Lazur can answer. They are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Your company may still have rules about sending workbook screenshots to any AI tool, so check those before you use it on payroll or supplier data.
Pricing and where to start

Lazur has a 3-day Pro trial with no credit card. The trial starts when you first open the app. Pro costs $18 a month, or $15 a month billed annually, and includes 250 AI actions. Power costs $120 a month, or $96 a month billed annually, and includes 1,000 AI actions. Dictation is unlimited on both plans. Check the [pricing page](/pricing) for current terms, then [download Lazur for Mac](/download).
If you want the Excel side first, the [Excel assistant page](/apps/excel) covers finding buttons, explaining formulas and learning pivot tables.
A short plan for this week

items: Turn each range in your capacity or reorder workbook into a named table.
Test a few shortcuts from the table above on a copy of the file.
Build the weekly load grid with one SUMIFS formula, then copy it across.
Ask Lazur where the filter button is, and follow its circle until you find it.

faq.question: Does Excel for Mac have every feature that Excel for Windows has?
faq.answer: Not always. Microsoft's October 2026 update lists no features that are exclusive to Mac, and names no Mac-specific menu changes. Some features reach Mac later. The Copilot skill recorder is still for Insiders on Mac. Check Microsoft's What's New in Excel posts for the feature you need.

faq.question: Which Excel version is current on Mac?
faq.answer: Microsoft does not publish a single numbered version this page can confirm for Mac. Open Excel > About Excel to see your build. Then compare it with the latest What's New in Excel post before you rely on a feature.

faq.question: Can Lazur click buttons or edit my workbook?
faq.answer: No. Lazur points at buttons, explains formulas, answers out loud, guides you one click at a time and drafts text. You do the clicking and the editing. When you hold fn, dictation types clean text at your cursor.

faq.question: Does Lazur work with Excel on Windows?
faq.answer: Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available. Lazur is not a plugin or add-in for any app. It runs as its own app on your Mac, beside Excel.

faq.question: Can I use Agent Mode in Excel on Mac?
faq.answer: It depends on your license and your region. Commercial Microsoft 365 Copilot licenses and Microsoft 365 Personal, Family and Premium subscriptions qualify. At launch it was not offered in the EU or the UK. Check current eligibility with Microsoft, because the Mac rollout date in its January post is unclear.

faq.question: Is my spreadsheet data sent to AI providers when I use Lazur?
faq.answer: Only what you show Lazur, and only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to produce an answer. They are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models. Check your company policy before you share payroll or supplier data.
